segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So I want to talk about something now that's different in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now first I want to speak about what this means.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Rather than an obstacle to learning, it's part of the experience of learning a new language which can make you realize that in your own language you are both permitted and obliged to perceive and express the world in a certain way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's two important kind of contradictory concepts here almost.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It permits you and obliges you, it allows you and requires you to perceive and to express the world in a certain way.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, in Spanish we have two verbs for "to be".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So remember "to be" is "is", "am", "are". We get all of this from "to be". We don't say "I be", we say "I am".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have ser—this is where es comes from, this is where son comes from—and ser is about characteristics, when we refer to the characteristics of something. Actually, un ser is "a being". We said that some form of the verb is often the noun, here it's the complete form. Un ser is a being.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un ser humano is what?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Human being.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A human being. And we could've found humano even though there's no rule to find humano, that word. We have "humanity". The words "-ity" end how in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Humanidad.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Humanidad. And then we could probably guess then that "human" is humano. Un ser humano is a human being. So ser refers to things that are characteristic of something.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Then estar, which is the other "to be", estar refers to states, states we are in. The word "state" is related to estar. So Spanish permits us, allows us, but also obliges us when we are perceiving and expressing the world around us to make a decision and to think about something: is this a state, or is it a characteristic? So this kind of sounds very abstract right now, so let's look at some examples.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "To be tired", do you think this is a state, or do you think it's a characteristic of you, to be tired? Is it a state you're in or is it characteristic of you?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It's a state.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Where you are, is it a state you are in or is it a characteristic of you, where you are?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: A state.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: A state. To be a good or a bad person, you think this is a characteristic of you or a state?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Characteristic. So, it's very, very important to kind of snub out now any temptation that you might have to simplify this to temporary and permanent. This is what most learners do and actually what many teachers do, simplify this concept to temporary and permanent, which if you think about it this way, will work most of the time, but not all of the time. We want to think in this way: is it a state or is it a characteristic? For example, if I say "I am a student",

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: it's not very permanent, is it? But, is it a state or a characteristic, my profession or my occupation?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: It should be a state you're in.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's temporary, but that doesn't make it a state, huh? Your profession, according to Spanish, is characteristic of you, even if you do it for 5 minutes.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: I guess it's the same for example you said before with the word "aggressive". Someone can be aggressive and they can change, so that stops it from being permanent, but it's still it's still a characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Exactly. And we will see actually some adjectives we can use with both ser and estar to give different meanings, but the great bulk of them go with one or the other. This is Spanish conceptually deciding whether it's a characteristic or a state, forcing us to make this differentiation and to express it. Let's look at the forms. Let's look at the forms of estar to begin.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, "I am" from estar is estoy. Estoy. So it ends -oy. We already saw another verb that ends -oy, which is voy, "I go" or "I'm going". Estoy.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estoy. Now "to be" is a a very irregular verb in most languages. Look at English. From "to be" we get "am", "is", "are", "was". But this is actually not so irregular. We have this little irregularity, -oy: estoy.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And the other irregularity that we have is that this verb is the only verb in the entire Spanish language that doesn't have the accent on the penultimate syllable in the present tense. So, it's not éstoy, it's estoy. The accent's on the ending. This hasn't happened until now, and it won't happen again. So we have estar, and from estar we have estoy. Now all of the other forms are regular. We build them how we would expect to, with the exception that the accent will be on the last syllable, and it's the only verb in the entire present tense that has this characteristic.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So, how would you say "he is", "she is", "it is", "you are" from estar, using estar?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Está.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Está. "They" or "for you guys"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Están.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And make it for "you" informal?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estás.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And for the "we" version the accent is where it should be because we're adding two syllables. So give me the "we" version.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Estamos. So that's it, that's your set: estoy, está, están, estás, estamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The word for "tired" is cansado. Cansado. C-a-n-s-a-d-o, cansado.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cansado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say "I am tired"? This this is a state.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy cansada. Estoy cansada.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy cansada. Good. "We are tired" talking about a mixed or a masculine group?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estamos cansados.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estamos cansados. What if you were all female group?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estamos cansadas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Now the word for "always" we said was siempre. Siempre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, if you say "I'm always tired", because "tired" as an adjective, as an idea, is a state, not a characteristic, because we are looking at that, whether it's a state or a characteristic, rather than is it permanent or is it temporary, we are using estar. So even if you say "I'm always tired", it doesn't matter, you still use estar. So siempre is very flexible in this sentence, you can put it anywhere. The emphasis is going to change when you move it, but it's legal anywhere. So how would you say "I'm always tired"?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy cansada siempre.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy cansada siempre. Estoy siempre cansada. Siempre estoy cansada. Or I would say cansado. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we want to resist the temptation to simplify this concept to temporary and permanent. We want to ask ourselves: is it a state or is it a characteristic? "To be tired", is it a state or is it a characteristic? If we simplify it to temporary and permanent, most of the time it's going to work, this simplification, but many times we're going to feel frustrated, feeling like there's something we don't understand because Spanish disagrees with us. If we have the concepts of characteristic and state, the few times Spanish disagrees with what we consider a characteristic and state, it's going to be an interesting point of perspective. For example, muerto. Muerto, which means?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dead.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dead. Good. We looked at this briefly before as a part of "mortgage" meaning death pact. Muerto, in Spanish, is a state. Death is a state. So if you was to say "I'm dead", you would use estar. So how would you say that?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Estoy muerta.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Estoy muerta. And I would say estoy muerto. And you can use it to say "I'm very tired" as well. Estoy muerta, estoy muerto, "I'm very tired". Good.
